text: Left coronary angiogram (LCA injection): the catheter tip engages the left main ostium; contrast fills the left main (LM), which bifurcates into the LAD and the LCx. Two or more large branches diverge from a short common trunk.

Right coronary angiogram (RCA injection): a single long vessel with a C-shaped (LAO view) or L-shaped (RAO view) course along the atrioventricular groove; no bifurcation into two large branches near the catheter tip. Distally it gives the posterior descending artery (PDA) and posterolateral branches.

In a single injection only one coronary system is opacified: either the left system (LM, LAD, LCx) or the right system (RCA). Do not report LAD or LCx in a right coronary injection, and do not report RCA in a left coronary injection.

SYNTAX segments of the RCA: 1 proximal RCA (ostium to half of the way to the acute margin), 2 mid RCA, 3 distal RCA (to the origin of the PDA), 4 posterior descending artery (PDA), 16, 16a, 16b, 16c posterolateral branches from the RCA.
SYNTAX segment 5: left main coronary artery (LM), from the ostium to the bifurcation into LAD and LCx. It is short (about 1-2 cm) and lies closest to the catheter tip in a left injection.

SYNTAX segments of the LAD: 6 proximal LAD (to the first major septal), 7 mid LAD (to the second diagonal), 8 apical LAD; 9 and 9a first diagonal branches, 10 and 10a second diagonal branches. The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex and gives septal branches (downward) and diagonal branches (laterally).

SYNTAX segments of the LCx: 11 proximal circumflex, 13 distal circumflex, 12, 12a, 12b obtuse marginal branches, 14, 14a, 14b left posterolateral branches, 15 posterior descending branch from the LCx (in left dominance). The LCx runs in the left atrioventricular groove.

Standard projections: RAO caudal shows the LM bifurcation, proximal LCx and obtuse marginals well; RAO cranial and AP cranial show the mid and distal LAD with diagonals separated; LAO caudal (spider view) shows the LM and proximal LAD/LCx; LAO for the RCA shows a C-shaped proximal and mid RCA.

Orientation cues: the LAD usually courses toward the apex along the anterior interventricular groove and is the vessel with septal branches; the LCx curves along the atrioventricular groove and gives marginal branches toward the lateral wall. Overlapping vessels and foreshortening make segment boundaries uncertain.

Coronary dominance is defined by the artery that gives the PDA: right dominance (about 70-80% of people, PDA from RCA, segment 4), left dominance (PDA from LCx, segment 15), co-dominance. Dominance cannot be determined reliably from a single injection.

Angiographic stenosis appears as a focal narrowing of the contrast-filled lumen relative to adjacent reference segments: an hourglass narrowing, an abrupt step-down in caliber, a filling defect, or an abrupt vessel cut-off (occlusion). Gradual tapering toward the distal vessel is normal and is not a stenosis.

Stenosis severity by visual diameter estimation: below 50% mild (not significant), 50-69% moderate, 70-99% severe, 100% total occlusion. A stenosis of 50% or more in the left main, or 70% or more in other epicardial vessels, is considered significant.

Pitfalls that mimic stenosis: vessel overlap, foreshortening, branch origins, catheter-induced spasm, myocardial bridging (systolic compression of the LAD), and streaming of incompletely mixed contrast. Report a stenosis only when the narrowing is visible on the image.

Structured angiographic report: for each artery and segment state whether it is visualized, whether a stenosis is present, its estimated severity, and its location. If a segment is not visible in the projection, state that it cannot be assessed instead of guessing.
Each finding should be tied to a specific location on the image. When the image quality, contrast filling or projection is insufficient, the finding should be marked as uncertain or not assessable.
